raw_response:
I farm only 4.5 mu, so even though I understand the technical recommendations, I still make decisions like a smallholder first: protect yield, control cash spending, and fit the work around my family's off-farm jobs. In Quzhou, the wheat-maize rotation is still the safest system for me. I am not going to make any big change this year. Wheat is the main crop for holding stable output through winter and spring, and maize follows immediately after harvest, so I need a plan that keeps the turnaround fast. Because I have well irrigation, I can support the crop at the key stages, but pumping costs money, so I will not irrigate more than necessary.

For wheat, I will stay with an improved local variety that performs reliably here rather than chasing a new one. With my experience, the key is to establish a full stand in October, put enough base fertilizer down to support tillering, and then topdress once at jointing depending on crop color and winter survival. Since fertilizer prices and irrigation costs are always a burden, I would rather keep nitrogen at a solid middle level than push for the very top yield target. For maize, I will sow as soon as the wheat is harvested, within a few days, because the time window is tight and delay costs more yield than almost anything else. I will simplify tillage after wheat, use one main fertilizer application and one topdress, and give irrigation only if rainfall is short at the critical stages. That is the balance I trust: not the maximum input plan, but a stable, workable one for my land and labor.
